[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal study of mentoring interactions in remote-work settings, comparing career progression metrics (e.g., promotion rates, mentorship access) across underrepresented groups with varying levels of scheduling flexibility. — Directly tests the causal link between unequal scheduling flexibility and career advancement inequity by tracking real-world outcomes over time.

[PATH:empirical] Survey-based research on perceived availability of informal vs. scheduled mentoring among underrepresented groups in remote-work environments, including measures of flexibility and career support. — Captures subjective experience and self-reported inequities, helping to confirm whether the shift to scheduled mentoring is perceived as disadvantaging those with less flexibility.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical modeling of network effects and opportunity structures in remote work, drawing on social capital theory and organizational equity frameworks. — Provides a conceptual basis for understanding how unequal scheduling flexibility might amplify existing disparities in mentoring access and career advancement, and can generate testable predictions.

qualifier.temporal: since the widespread adoption of remote work in 2020
qualifier.geographic: global, with emphasis on regions with high remote work adoption

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal survey of career outcomes for underrepresented groups in tech firms pre- and post-2020, controlling for schedule flexibility and mentoring access. — Directly tests whether scheduled mentoring correlates with differential career advancement for underrepresented groups, and whether schedule flexibility moderates this effect.

[PATH:empirical] Organizational network analysis of mentoring tie formation in remote vs. in-office knowledge workers, using metadata from communication platforms (e.g., Slack, Teams) to quantify spontaneous vs. scheduled mentoring interactions. — Provides behavioral data to confirm whether remote work reduces spontaneous mentoring and whether this reduction disproportionately affects employees with less flexible schedules.

[PATH:literature] Review of equity-focused literature on remote work, mentoring, and career advancement (e.g., studies on virtual mentoring bias, schedule flexibility disparities, and intersectional effects). — Synthesizes existing findings to assess the plausibility of the hypothesis and identify gaps where new empirical work is needed.

[PATH:empirical] Network analysis study of informal sponsorship ties in a large multinational corporation pre- and post-2020, using email metadata or Slack communication logs to measure ad-hoc visibility changes — Provides quantitative evidence on whether remote work reduces spontaneous interactions that lead to sponsorship, and whether this effect is larger for underrepresented employees.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing literature on remote work, mentoring, and career advancement disparities (e.g., from journals like 'Journal of Vocational Behavior' or 'Academy of Management Annals') — Synthesizes available evidence to assess the consistency of the hypothesized effect across contexts, and identifies gaps that new empirical work should address.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal study comparing career progression metrics (e.g., promotions, salary growth) between underrepresented groups in organizations that transitioned from ad-hoc to scheduled remote mentoring programs versus those that maintained informal mentoring. — Directly tests the causal claim by measuring career advancement outcomes under structured vs. spontaneous mentoring conditions, controlling for other variables.

[PATH:empirical] Survey-based research on perceived equity and access to mentorship among underrepresented remote workers, capturing self-reported frequency, quality, and scheduling of mentoring interactions. — Provides subjective validation of whether scheduled mentoring reduces access disparities and enhances perceived career support, complementing objective metrics.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing literature on structured mentoring programs in remote work contexts, focusing on outcomes for underrepresented groups (e.g., women, racial/ethnic minorities) in post-2020 global settings. — Synthesizes prior findings to assess consistency with the hypothesis and identify moderators (e.g., industry, mentorship duration) that may affect the relationship.
